newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Amsterdam bourse seen peaking, but no sharp fall.
newsitem.headline: Amsterdam bourse seen peaking, but no sharp fall.

text.p: The Amsterdam stock market has enjoyed a dramatic rise on the back of Wall Street's rally this year but strategists reckon the AEX index is nearing its peak, although it is likely to be cushioned from any sharp correction.

"The Dutch market is still in excellent shape, all the signs are positive -- interest rates are low and may decline further," Philip Menco, chief strategist at ING Barings Research, said on Wednesday.
The AEX index of blue-chip Dutch stocks hit an all-time record close on Tuesday at 592.45 points, a 25 percent rise this year and more than 50 percent above where it was 18 months ago.
"We have come such a long way in the past two years, it is difficult to see too much potential left," Menco added.
Others were similarly cautious over the medium-term outlook.
"I'm not sure thare's a lot of potential left. We could be overdoing a little," said Rutger Terluin, economist at Amstgeld.

But dealers said money inflows into the Dutch market were still strong and the positive outlook for the economy was likely to keep shares buoyant. Analysts forecast an average increase in Dutch corporate earnings of 12 to 13 percent next year.

Menco said he was maintaining a six to 12-month forecast for the AEX at 610 points and he expected this to be reached "sooner rather than later." But he warned of a short-term dash for the psychologically-key 600 point level.
"Empirical studies tell us a round number cannot be held onto. The market has to get past there or it will fall back."
But, as the outlook for European economies remains relatively rosy, the same is not true for the United States and any correction there would have a knock-on effect here.
Analysts said that while they could envisage a five to 10 percent correction on Wall Street they did not expect the Dutch market to fall by the same amount.

"I think the Federal Reserve will raise rates in either December or early next year. That could put the brakes on things," Terluin said. "But the correction on European markets shouldn't be as large as in the States."
Menco agreed that the major risk to the Dutch market came from the United States where the possibility of higher interest rates and disappointing earnings could wipe up to 10 percent off Wall Street.
"This would hurt the Amsterdam market." he said.
